name: Free-Choice Fused Relative in -ever

1.definition: Picks out an eligible participant without requiring the speaker to identify which one.

examples.form: [Whoever is on duty] can sign it.

projection.target: In a generic or future context the identity can be left open. The whole phrase occupies an NP position and can also have a specific unknown referent in a suitable episodic context.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Whoever and whatever as noun phrases
curious.summary: A word like whoever starts a phrase that picks out someone eligible, without saying who.
curious.body:
In Whoever is on duty can sign it, the speaker picks out a person by a condition rather than by name. The speaker doesn't need to know who that is.

The whole phrase, whoever is on duty, fills a noun's place in the sentence. In a general or future situation the identity can stay open. In a suitable one-off situation it can also point to one specific person the speaker doesn't know.

examples.text: [Whoever is on duty] can sign it.

curious.try: Say Whoever is on duty can sign it. Does the speaker need to know who is on duty?

teacher.summary: Helps explain -ever phrases like whoever is on duty, which pick out an unspecified eligible person or thing.
teacher.explain: A free-choice fused relative is an NP made of a relative wh-ever word plus a dependent clause. It picks out an eligible participant without requiring the speaker to identify which one. In a generic or future context the identity can be left open, and the whole phrase occupies an NP position. In a suitable episodic context it can also have a specific unknown referent. This dictionary treats it as a specialization of the fused relative NP, distinct from the unconditional wh-adjunct, and marks it provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: Fused relative is CGEL's term. Free relative is a common textbook name.

examples.text: [Whoever is on duty] can sign it.

watch_for: A learner might think the speaker must know who is on duty.
A learner might look for a separate noun that whoever modifies, when the whole phrase fills an NP position.
teacher.activity: Students complete sentences beginning Whoever, Whatever or Whichever, giving each a role in the sentence (subject or object). They then say whether the speaker needs to know who or what is meant.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Free-Choice Fused Relative in -ever." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/fused-relative-no-matter-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, fa37529).
